full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: The plaintiff presented the appeal against the decree dated 30-7-2000 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1 at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 82 of 1997, which dismissed the suit. 

 2. On 28-5-95 the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 166 of 1995 for eviction of defendant No. 1 from the suit land measuring about 300 square yards with structures thereon comprising of Plot # 8, Road # 3 of Block # A at Section # 10 of Mirpur Housing Estate fully described in the schedule to the plaint. On increase of the valuation, the suit was, on transfer to the aforesaid Court of Subordinate Judge, renumbered as Title Suit No. 82 of 1997. 

 3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to SA recorded tenant Abdur Rashid Matabbor, an uncle of the appellant. The Government acquired the suit land along with other property for Mirpur Housing Estate. After requisition and acquisition the government did not take over physical possession and, as such, the suit land remained in the possession of said Abdur Rashid Matabbor till his death. 

 4. Abdur Rashid died leaving three sons namely, Abdul Mannan, Abdur Rahman and Abdul Karim. They settled the suit land along with other property with the plaintiff and delivered possession. The plaintiff also got allotment of the suit plot from the Government. At the time of delivery of possession defendant No. 1 was occupying the tin shed as a caretaker. He was allowed to continue as such. On 27-6-94 on behalf of Mirpur Housing Estate possession was also delivered to the plaintiff. After mutation of his name the plaintiff possessed the suit property by payment of rents, taxes, etc. 

 5. On 27-1-95, when the plaintiff asked defendant No. 1 to vacate for construction, defendant No. 1 refused and resisted. Hence the suit. 

 7. Defendant No. 1 claimed that the suit as framed in the form and manner was not maintainable and also hit by provisions of Specific Relief Act. Defendant No. 1 was not evictable from the suit property. 

 8. His definite case was that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acquired the suit land for Mirpur satellite town. On the prayer of Mohammad Jabbar the suit plot was on 17-9-63 allotted to him and delivered possession. Said Jabbar made a tin shed and lived there with his family. On 11-2-75 Jabbar orally gifted the suit plot to defendant No. 1 and delivered possession. Since then defendant No. 1 possessed the suit land by opening a municipal holding and obtaining electric line, water line and gas connection and living therein with his family. He made three more tin sheds and let them out to tenants. The suit land was never allotted to the plaintiff. In the suit plot the plaintiff had no title. 

 9. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in their written statement stated that on 5-5-94 the suit land was allotted to the plaintiff. On 20-7-94 possession was delivered, On 19-10-95 lease deed was registered and on 23-4-95 name of plaintiff was mutated. Subsequently, as there was mistake in the allotment, residential plot was allotted and on 27-7-95 the lease deed was registered. Name of Jabbar Kadri could not be found in respect of the suit land. They claimed that the claim of defendant No. 1 was not correct. 

 10. The parties lead evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. 

 11. The appellant has come up with an application under Order XXIII, rule 1(2) read with section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure for withdrawal of the appeal as well as the suit with permission to sue afresh. 

 12. Mr Ozair Farook, learned Senior Advocate on behalf of the appellant, submits that the suit was poorly drafted by a Mofussil lawyer and forgot to pray for declaration of title in the suit land. He submitted that in the absence of such prayer the suit was doomed to fail and, in fact, failed; 

 14. Mr Md Nazibur Rahman, learned Senior Advocate for the respondent No. 1, submitted that after dismissal of the suit even on the question of title the application did not deserve consideration otherwise the plaintiff would be allowed to commence fresh litigation on the same cause of action. He took us through the judgment and submitted that learned Subordinate Judge already found that the plaintiff failed to prove his title, interest in the suit land. 

 16. Sub-rule 1 of rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure entitles a plaintiff to withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim at any time after institution of the suit. 

 17. Such provision is now well settled to enable an appeilant as well to withdraw the appeal along with the suit. 

 18. Sub-rule 2 of rule I of said Order empowers a court to allow a plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the same subject matter of a suit Or part of claim if it is satisfied that the suit would fail by reason of some 'formal defect' or for some 'other sufficient grounds. 

 19. What is 'formal defect' has not been defined anywhere in the Code. But there are good authorities that the expression formal defect should receive wide and liberal meaning. Even when a plaintiff could not be allowed to Withdraw his suit with liberty to sue afresh on the ground of any 'formal defect' the Court may still allow him to do so on any other ground sufficient for satisfaction of the Court. The expression other sufficient grounds does not appear to have been used by the legislature as ejusdem generis with the expression formal defect. 

 20. The legal meaning of the word formal is done in due form or with solemnity; according to regular way. The expression, formal defect connotes defects of diverse kinds not affecting the merit of the case but arising out of some error made in good faith. It is a defect of form prescribed by the rules of procedure. If it goes to the root of the suit, it is not a formal defect. Even when there was no such formal defect the Court is not powerless to grant the same prayer if justice demands. 

 21. So, ultimate discretion rests with the Court. the Court should only guard that the plaintiff should not be allowed another opportunity to commence a fresh trial after he failed to conduct the suit with care and diligence; (Madan Mohan Pal vs Abdus Samad 32 DLR 176). 

 22. If the suit was disposed of and ultimately dismissed on merits then the plaintiff would not be entitled to have the liberty to sue afresh on the same subject matter (Gurnek Singh and another vs Gurbachan Singh and others, AIR 1986 Panjab and Hariana 228. 

 23. In Atul vs Raukishore AIR 1956 Orissa 77, a suit was instituted for accounts but without any relief prayed for dissolution of partnership. A single bench found that failure of the Advocate to incorporate a prayer for dissolution of the partnership was bound to result in dismissal of the suit. That was a defect and provides a sufficient ground for permitting the plaintiff to come to the Court again with a properly drafted plaint. 

 24. In Muhammad Din vs Atta Muhammad, PLD 1957 (WP) Lahore 971, a single bench upheld the order of the trial Court allowing withdrawal of the suit on the reasoning that the omission in the plaint of the fact that the parties were governed by custom was not intentional. In the absence of such averment in the plaint, the plaintiff ran grave risk of being non-suited, The plaintiffs should not be made to suffer for the negligence of their Counsel in not drafting a proper plaint. 

 25. In lsmail vs Fida Ali, PLD 1965 SC 634 = 17 DLR (SC) 531 the Supreme Court of Pakistan on the oral prayer of the learned, Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent granted leave for withdrawal of the suit against the defendant with permission to file a fresh suit. The suit was based on endorsement simpliciter and the endorsement appeared on the back of a promissory note. The suit was found bound to fail in the form as framed. The suit was decreed by a single Judge. 

 26. On careful perusal of the plaint we find that learned Advocate could not be sure as to how to seek the relief in the facts and circumstances of the case. There is more than one amendment by both parties. Even thereafter, when in the written statement of the defendant No. 1 it was clearly claimed that the suit as framed was not maintainable and also hit by the provision of the Specific Relief Act it did not occur to him that he should seek a declaration of title. It is true that there is a finding on title by the trial Court but such finding must be taken to be incidental to the finding on the relief for recovery of possession only. 

 27. When the title of the plaintiff was seriously contested simple suit for eviction was doomed to fail. And seeking a decree of declaration of title, the plaintiff is required to state clearly the history of title as he could trace. 

 28. In the circumstances, we are of the view if the appellant is not allowed to sue afresh for a decree of declaration of title he would be deprived of an opportunity to vindicate his right to the property in question. The application therefore merits consideration.
